solutions.question: An eagle dives to the ground along a 300 m path with an average speed of 60 m s⁻¹. How long does it take to cover this distance?
steps: Total distance covered = S = 300 m
Average speed = v_av = 60 m s⁻¹
Total time taken = t = ?
Using the equation v_av = S/t
or t = S/v_av
putting the values t = 300 m/(60 m s⁻¹) = 5 s
solutions.answer: 5 s

solutions.question: Define scalar and vector quantities.
steps: A scalar quantity is a physical quantity which has magnitude only and no direction.
A vector quantity is a physical quantity which has both magnitude and direction.
solutions.answer: A scalar has magnitude only; a vector has magnitude and direction.

solutions.question: Give 5 examples each for scalar and vector quantities.
steps: Examples of scalar quantities: distance, speed, time, mass and temperature.
Examples of vector quantities: displacement, velocity, acceleration, force and weight.
solutions.answer: Scalars: distance, speed, time, mass and temperature. Vectors: displacement, velocity, acceleration, force and weight.

solutions.question: State head-to-tail rule for addition of vectors.
steps: To add vectors by the head-to-tail rule, place the tail of the second vector at the head of the first vector.
The resultant vector is drawn from the tail of the first vector to the head of the last vector.
solutions.answer: Join the vectors head to tail; the resultant extends from the first tail to the last head.

solutions.question: What are distance- time graph and speed-time graph?
steps: A distance-time graph represents the distance covered by a body with respect to time.
A speed-time graph represents the speed of a body with respect to time.
solutions.answer: A distance-time graph shows distance against time; a speed-time graph shows speed against time.

solutions.question: Falling objects near the Earth have the same constant acceleration. Does this imply that a heavier object will fall faster than a lighter object?
steps: No. The same constant acceleration of falling objects does not mean that a heavier object falls faster than a lighter object.
In the absence of air resistance, all objects near the Earth fall with the same acceleration, regardless of their masses.
solutions.answer: No. Without air resistance, heavy and light objects fall with the same acceleration.

solutions.question: The vector quantities are sometimes written in scalar notation (not bold face). How is the direction indicated?
steps: When a vector is written in scalar notation, its direction is indicated by a plus (+) or minus (−) sign with respect to a chosen reference direction.
solutions.answer: Its direction is indicated by a plus or minus sign relative to a chosen reference direction.

solutions.question: A body is moving with uniform speed. Will its velocity be uniform? Give reason.
steps: No, not necessarily.
Velocity is uniform only when both speed and direction remain constant.
A body moving with uniform speed may change its direction; therefore, its velocity may change.
solutions.answer: Uniform speed does not necessarily mean uniform velocity, because the direction may change.

solutions.question: Is it possible for a body to have acceleration? When moving with: (i) constant velocity (ii) constant speed
steps: (i) A body moving with constant velocity has no acceleration, because its velocity does not change.
(ii) A body moving with constant speed may have acceleration if its direction changes, as in circular motion.
If it moves with constant speed in a straight line without changing direction, its acceleration is zero.
solutions.answer: Constant velocity means zero acceleration; constant speed can have acceleration if direction changes.

solutions.question: Distance and displacement may or may not be equal in magnitude. Explain this statement.
steps: Distance is the total length of the actual path travelled by an object, whereas displacement is the shortest straight-line distance from its initial to its final position in a specified direction.
If an object moves along a straight line in one direction, the magnitude of its distance and displacement are equal.
If an object changes direction or follows a curved path, the magnitude of its distance is greater than the magnitude of its displacement.
solutions.answer: Distance and displacement are equal in magnitude for straight-line motion in one direction; otherwise, distance is greater.

solutions.question: When a bullet is fired, its velocity with which it leaves the barrel is called the muzzle velocity of the gun. The muzzle velocity of one gun with a longer barrel is lesser than that of another gun with a shorter barrel. In which gun is the acceleration of the bullet larger? Explain your answer.
steps: Assume the bullet starts from rest and has uniform acceleration while moving through the barrel.
For motion with uniform acceleration, v² = u² + 2as. Since u = 0, a = v²/(2s).
The gun with the longer barrel produces a lower muzzle velocity, while its barrel length is greater.
Therefore, its value of v²/(2s) is smaller. The bullet's acceleration is larger in the gun with the shorter barrel.
solutions.answer: The bullet's acceleration is larger in the gun with the shorter barrel.

solutions.question: For a complete trip, average velocity was calculated. Its value came out to be positive. Is it possible that its instantaneous velocity at any time during the trip had the negative value? Give justification of your answer.
steps: Yes, it is possible.
A positive average velocity for the complete trip means that the net displacement is in the positive direction.
The object may move in the negative direction during part of the trip and still have a positive net displacement for the complete trip.
Therefore, its instantaneous velocity may be negative at some time during the trip.
solutions.answer: Yes. Instantaneous velocity can be negative during part of a trip even when average velocity for the complete trip is positive.

solutions.question: A ball is thrown vertically upward with velocity v. It returns to the ground in time T. Which of the following graphs correctly represents the motion? Explain your reasoning.
steps: For upward motion, take the upward direction as positive.
The ball has initial velocity +v and constant acceleration −g due to gravity.
Its velocity decreases uniformly with time, becomes zero at the highest point, and then becomes negative as the ball falls.
Thus, the correct velocity–time graph is a straight line with negative slope, starting at +v, crossing the time axis at T/2, and ending at −v at time T.
solutions.answer: The correct velocity–time graph is a straight line from +v at t = 0 to −v at t = T, crossing zero at T/2.

solutions.question: The figure given below shows the distance - time graph for the travel of a cyclist. Find the velocities for the segments a, b and c.
steps: The distance–time graph referred to in the question is not included, so the numerical velocities of segments a, b and c cannot be determined.
The velocity for each segment is found from the slope of that segment of the distance–time graph: velocity = change in distance / change in time.
A steeper segment represents a greater velocity; a horizontal segment represents zero velocity.
solutions.answer: The velocities cannot be calculated without the graph and its scale; each is the slope of its segment.

solutions.question: Is it possible that the velocity of an object is zero at an instant of time, but its acceleration is not zero? If yes, give an example of such a case.
steps: Yes, it is possible for the velocity of an object to be zero at an instant while its acceleration is not zero.
For example, when a ball is thrown vertically upward, its velocity is zero for an instant at the highest point.
At that instant, its acceleration is still g downward due to gravity.
solutions.answer: Yes. At the highest point of a vertically thrown ball, velocity is momentarily zero but acceleration is g downward.

solutions.question: How a vector can be represented graphically? Explain.
steps: A vector is represented graphically by a directed line segment.
The length of the line segment, drawn according to a suitable scale, represents the magnitude of the vector.
The arrowhead shows the direction of the vector.
The vector is labelled with its symbol.
solutions.answer: A vector is shown by a scaled directed line segment: its length represents magnitude and its arrowhead represents direction.

solutions.question: Differentiate between: (a) rest and motion
steps: Rest: An object is at rest if its position does not change with time relative to its surroundings.
Motion: An object is in motion if its position changes with time relative to its surroundings.
Rest and motion are relative terms; an object may be at rest relative to one body and in motion relative to another.
solutions.answer: An object is at rest if its position does not change with time relative to its surroundings, and in motion if it does.

solutions.question: Differentiate between: (b) speed and velocity
steps: Speed is the distance covered by an object in unit time.
Velocity is the displacement of an object in unit time in a specified direction.
Speed is a scalar quantity; it has magnitude only.
Velocity is a vector quantity; it has both magnitude and direction.
solutions.answer: Speed is distance per unit time and a scalar; velocity is displacement per unit time in a specified direction and a vector.

solutions.question: Describe different types of motion. Also give examples.
steps: Motion is of three types: translatory motion, rotatory motion and vibratory motion.
In translatory motion, a body moves from one place to another. Its particles move the same distance in the same direction in a given time.

Translatory motion may be linear, circular or random. A car moving along a straight road shows linear motion; a stone tied to a string and whirled shows circular motion; and the motion of gas molecules shows random motion.
In rotatory motion, a body spins about an axis passing through it. The spinning of a fan is an example.
In vibratory motion, a body moves to and fro about its mean position. The motion of a simple pendulum is an example.
solutions.answer: The three types of motion are translatory, rotatory and vibratory motion; examples include a moving car, a spinning fan and a simple pendulum, respectively.

solutions.question: Explain the difference between distance and displacement.
steps: Distance is the length of the actual path covered by a moving body.
Displacement is the shortest distance between the initial and final positions of a body in a specified direction.
Distance is a scalar quantity, whereas displacement is a vector quantity.
Distance is always positive, while displacement may be positive, negative or zero.
The magnitude of displacement is always less than or equal to the distance travelled.
solutions.answer: Distance is the actual path length; displacement is the shortest directed distance from the initial to the final position.

solutions.question: What do gradients of distance-time graph and speed-time graph represent? Explain it by drawing diagrams.
Prove that the area under speed-time graph is equal to the distance covered by an object.
steps: Consider an object moving with uniform speed v for time t.
Distance covered, s = speed × time = vt.
The area under its speed-time graph is the area of a rectangle.
Area = base × height = t × v = vt.
Therefore, the area under the speed-time graph is equal to the distance covered. For a changing speed, the area under the graph gives the total distance covered.
solutions.answer: The area under a speed-time graph represents the distance covered by the object.

solutions.question: How equations of motion can be applied to the bodies moving under the action of gravity?
steps: For a body moving under gravity, the acceleration a in the equations of motion is replaced by the acceleration due to gravity g.
The equations of motion become: v = u + gt; s = ut + ½gt²; v² = u² + 2gs.
These equations apply when downward is taken as the positive direction.
If upward is taken as positive, the acceleration is −g, so g is replaced by −g in the equations.
solutions.answer: For motion under gravity, use the equations of motion with a = g (or a = −g when upward is positive).

solutions.question: Draw the representative lines of the following vectors: (a) A velocity of 400 m s⁻¹ making an angle of 60° with x-axis.
steps: Choose the scale 1 cm = 100 m s⁻¹.
Draw the positive x-axis as the reference direction.
From the origin, measure 60° anticlockwise from the positive x-axis and draw a 4 cm line in that direction.
Put an arrowhead at the end and label the line 400 m s⁻¹.
solutions.answer: The representative line is 4 cm long at 60° to the positive x-axis, labelled 400 m s⁻¹, using the scale 1 cm = 100 m s⁻¹.

drawn.title: Velocity vector
drawn.description: Draw the representative line 4 cm long, at 60° anticlockwise from the positive x-axis. Scale: 1 cm = 100 m s⁻¹. Add an arrowhead and label it 400 m s⁻¹.

solutions.question: Draw the representative lines of the following vectors: (b) A force of 50 N making an angle of 120° with x-axis.
steps: Choose the scale 1 cm = 10 N.
Draw the positive x-axis as the reference direction.
From the origin, measure 120° anticlockwise from the positive x-axis and draw a 5 cm line in that direction.
Put an arrowhead at the end and label the line 50 N.
solutions.answer: The representative line is 5 cm long at 120° to the positive x-axis, labelled 50 N, using the scale 1 cm = 10 N.

drawn.title: Force vector
drawn.description: Draw the representative line 5 cm long, at 120° anticlockwise from the positive x-axis. Scale: 1 cm = 10 N. Add an arrowhead and label it 50 N.

solutions.question: A car is moving with an average speed of 72 km h⁻¹. How much time will it take to cover a distance of 360 km?
steps: Given: Average speed, v = 72 km h⁻¹ = 20 m s⁻¹; distance, d = 360 km = 360000 m.
Required: Time, t.
Formula: t = d / v.
Substitution: t = 360000 m / 20 m s⁻¹.
Working: t = 18000 s = 5 h.
Result: The car will take 5 h.
solutions.answer: 5 h

solutions.question: A truck starts from rest. It reaches a velocity of 90 km h⁻¹ in 50 seconds. Find its average acceleration.
steps: Given: Initial velocity, u = 0 m s⁻¹; final velocity, v = 90 km h⁻¹ = 25 m s⁻¹; time, t = 50 s.
Required: Average acceleration, a.
Formula: a = (v − u) / t.
Substitution: a = (25 m s⁻¹ − 0 m s⁻¹) / 50 s.
Working: a = 25 / 50 = 0.5 m s⁻².
Result: The average acceleration is 0.5 m s⁻².
solutions.answer: 0.5 m s⁻²

solutions.question: A car passes a green traffic signal while moving with a velocity of 5 m s⁻¹. It then accelerates to 1.5 m s⁻². What is the velocity of car after 5 seconds?
steps: Given: Initial velocity, u = 5 m s⁻¹; acceleration, a = 1.5 m s⁻²; time, t = 5 s.
Required: Final velocity, v.
Formula: v = u + at.
Substitution: v = 5 m s⁻¹ + (1.5 m s⁻² × 5 s).
Working: v = 5 m s⁻¹ + 7.5 m s⁻¹ = 12.5 m s⁻¹.
Result: The velocity of the car after 5 s is 12.5 m s⁻¹.

solutions.question: A motorcycle initially travelling at 18 km h⁻¹ accelerates at constant rate of 2 m s⁻². How far will the motorcycle go in 10 seconds?
steps: Given: Initial velocity, u = 18 km h⁻¹ = 5 m s⁻¹; acceleration, a = 2 m s⁻²; time, t = 10 s.
Required: Distance travelled, s.
Formula: s = ut + ½at².
Substitution: s = (5 m s⁻¹ × 10 s) + ½(2 m s⁻² × (10 s)²).
Working: s = 50 m + 100 m = 150 m.
Result: The motorcycle will travel 150 m.

solutions.question: A wagon is moving on the road with a velocity of 54 km h⁻¹. Brakes are applied suddenly. The wagon covers a distance of 25 m before stopping. Determine the acceleration of the wagon.
steps: Given: Initial velocity, u = 54 km h⁻¹ = 15 m s⁻¹; final velocity, v = 0 m s⁻¹; distance, s = 25 m.
Required: Acceleration, a.
Formula: v² = u² + 2as.
Substitution: (0 m s⁻¹)² = (15 m s⁻¹)² + 2a(25 m).
Working: 0 = 225 + 50a; therefore, a = −225 / 50 = −4.5 m s⁻².
Result: The acceleration of the wagon is −4.5 m s⁻².

solutions.question: A stone is dropped from a height of 45 m. How long will it take to reach the ground? What will be its velocity just before hitting the ground?
steps: Given: Initial velocity, u = 0 m s⁻¹; distance fallen, s = 45 m; acceleration due to gravity, g = 10 m s⁻².
Required: Time taken, t, and final velocity, v.
Formula: s = ut + ½gt²; v = u + gt.
Substitution: 45 m = (0 m s⁻¹ × t) + ½(10 m s⁻² × t²).
Working: 45 = 5t²; t² = 9; therefore, t = 3 s. Then v = 0 + (10 m s⁻² × 3 s) = 30 m s⁻¹.
Result: The stone takes 3 s to reach the ground and its velocity just before hitting the ground is 30 m s⁻¹.
solutions.answer: 3 s, 30 m s⁻¹

solutions.question: A car travels 10 km with an average velocity of 20 m s⁻¹. Then it travels in the same direction through a diversion at an average velocity of 4 m s⁻¹ for the next 0.8 km. Determine the average velocity of the car for the total journey.
steps: Given: First distance, d₁ = 10 km = 10000 m; first average velocity, v₁ = 20 m s⁻¹; second distance, d₂ = 0.8 km = 800 m; second average velocity, v₂ = 4 m s⁻¹.
Required: Average velocity for the total journey, v̄.
Formula: v̄ = total displacement / total time.
Substitution: t₁ = d₁ / v₁ = 10000 m / 20 m s⁻¹ = 500 s; t₂ = d₂ / v₂ = 800 m / 4 m s⁻¹ = 200 s.
Working: Total displacement = 10000 m + 800 m = 10800 m; total time = 500 s + 200 s = 700 s. Therefore, v̄ = 10800 m / 700 s = 15.4 m s⁻¹.
Result: The average velocity of the car for the total journey is 15.4 m s⁻¹.

solutions.question: A ball is dropped from the top of a tower. The ball reaches the ground in 5 seconds. Find the height of the tower and the velocity of the ball with which it strikes the ground.
steps: Given: Initial velocity, u = 0 m s⁻¹; time, t = 5 s; acceleration due to gravity, g = 10 m s⁻².
Required: Height of the tower, s, and velocity of the ball when it strikes the ground, v.
Formula: s = ut + ½gt²; v = u + gt.
Substitution: s = (0 m s⁻¹ × 5 s) + ½(10 m s⁻² × (5 s)²).
Working: s = 125 m. Also, v = 0 + (10 m s⁻² × 5 s) = 50 m s⁻¹.
Result: The height of the tower is 125 m and the ball strikes the ground with a velocity of 50 m s⁻¹.

solutions.question: A cricket ball is hit so that it travels straight up in the air. An observer notes that it took 3 seconds to reach the highest point. What was the initial velocity of the ball? If the ball was hit 1 m above the ground, how high did it rise from the ground?
steps: Given: Time to reach highest point, t = 3 s; height above ground at which the ball was hit, h₀ = 1 m; acceleration due to gravity, g = 10 m s⁻² downward.
Required: Initial velocity, u; maximum height from the ground, H.
At the highest point, final velocity v = 0.
Using v = u − gt: u = v + gt.
Substitution: u = 0 m s⁻¹ + (10 m s⁻²)(3 s).
Working: u = 30 m s⁻¹.
Using s = ut − ½gt², the height risen above the point of launch is: s = (30 m s⁻¹)(3 s) − ½(10 m s⁻²)(3 s)².
Working: s = 90 m − 45 m = 45 m.
Maximum height from the ground: H = h₀ + s = 1 m + 45 m = 46 m.

mcqs.stem: The numerical ratio of displacement to distance is:
options: equal to or less than one
rationales: The ratio cannot always be less than one because displacement and distance are equal for straight-line motion without reversing direction.
The ratio is not always one because a change in direction can make the distance greater than the displacement.
The magnitude of displacement can never exceed the distance traveled, so this ratio cannot be greater than one.
The magnitude of displacement is at most the distance traveled, making the ratio equal to or less than one.

mcqs.stem: If a body does not change its position with respect to some fixed point, then it will be in a state of:
rationales: A body whose position does not change relative to a fixed point is at rest.
Motion means a change in position relative to a reference point, which is absent here.
Uniform motion involves continued movement at constant velocity, not an unchanged position.
Variable motion involves a change in velocity and therefore movement, not an unchanged position.

mcqs.stem: A ball is dropped from the top of a tower, the distance covered by it in the first second is:
rationales: In free fall from rest, the first-second distance is approximately ½ × 9.8 × 1² = 4.9 m, or 5 m.
The body falls about 5 m, not 10 m, in the first second.
The body falls about 5 m, not 50 m, in the first second.
The body falls about 5 m, not 100 m, in the first second.

mcqs.stem: A body accelerates from rest to a velocity of 144 km h⁻¹ in 20 seconds. The distance covered by it is:
rationales: The final speed is 40 m/s, so the average speed is 20 m/s and the distance in 20 s is 400 m, not 100 m.
With uniform acceleration from rest to 40 m/s, the average speed is 20 m/s and the distance is 20 × 20 = 400 m.
The distance is 400 m, not 1400 m.
The distance is 400 m, not 1440 m.

mcqs.stem: A body is moving with constant acceleration starting from rest. It covers a distance S in 4 seconds. How much time does it take to cover one-fourth of this distance?
rationales: For motion from rest with constant acceleration, distance is proportional to time squared, so one-fourth the distance takes 2 s, not 1 s.
Since S ∝ t², covering S/4 takes half of 4 s, which is 2 s.
Four seconds is the time to cover the full distance S, not one-fourth of it.
Sixteen seconds is not consistent with the fact that distance grows as the square of time.

mcqs.stem: The displacement time graphs of two objects A and B are shown in the figure. Point out the true statement from the following:
options: The velocity of A is greater than B.
The velocity of A is less than B.
The velocity of A is equal to that of B.
The graph gives no information in this regard.
rationales: The graph indicates that A has the steeper displacement-time slope, and slope represents velocity.
This is false because A's displacement-time slope is steeper than B's.
The velocities would be equal only if the two graph slopes were equal.
A displacement-time graph conveys velocity through its slope, so it does provide information about the velocities.

mcqs.stem: The area under the speed-time graph is numerically equal to:
rationales: The area under a speed-time graph represents distance, not velocity.
Uniform velocity is represented by a horizontal speed-time line, not by its area.
Acceleration is represented by the graph's gradient, not its area.
Speed multiplied by time gives distance, so the area under the speed-time graph is distance covered.

mcqs.stem: Gradient of the speed-time graph is equal to:
rationales: The vertical value on a speed-time graph is speed; its gradient is not speed.
The gradient of a speed-time graph gives acceleration, not velocity as the requested graph quantity.
The change in speed per unit time is acceleration, which is the graph's gradient.
The area under a speed-time graph gives distance, while its gradient gives acceleration.

mcqs.stem: Gradient of the distance-time graph is equal to the:
rationales: The gradient of a distance-time graph is change in distance per unit time, which is speed.
Velocity is the gradient of a displacement-time graph; this graph is specified as distance-time.
The graph's gradient is a rate of change, not the distance covered itself.
Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity and is not the gradient of a distance-time graph.

mcqs.stem: A car accelerates uniformly from 80.5 km h⁻¹ at t = 0 to 113 km h⁻¹ at t = 9 s. Which graph best describes the motion of the car?
options: (a) a rising curve that starts above the origin and bends upward
(b) a straight rising line from the origin
(c) a straight rising line that starts above the origin
(d) a straight falling line that starts above the origin and reaches the horizontal axis
rationales: Uniform acceleration produces a straight velocity-time line, not a curve.
The line must start above the origin because the initial speed is 80.5 km h⁻¹, not zero.
The speed increases uniformly from a nonzero initial value, so the graph is a straight rising line starting above the origin.
The speed increases rather than decreases, and it remains above zero throughout the stated interval.
